chapters.title: Chapter 2: Reading the Yield Curve and Rate Signals

lessons.title: Yield Curve 101: What an Inversion Actually Signals

body.text: A yield curve inversion is a market forecast, not a causal mechanism. Reading it correctly means understanding why the market is saying what it's saying, not just whether short rates exceed long ones.

children.text: Chapter 1 built the framework: phases, indicator categories, and why textbook cycle theory needs adjustment for India. Chapter 2 starts applying that framework to the first, and most widely quoted, class of leading indicator: rate and credit-market signals. This lesson covers the yield curve itself, why an inversion is treated as a recession warning in developed markets, and why that same signal needs real adjustment before you can use it in India.
What the Yield Curve Actually Plots

markDefs.definition: The extra yield investors demand for locking money into a longer-maturity bond instead of rolling over a series of shorter ones, compensating for the extra interest-rate and liquidity risk of a longer holding period.

children.text: A yield curve plots the yields of bonds from the same issuer, almost always the sovereign, across different maturities at a single point in time: 3-month, 1-year, 2-year, 5-year, 10-year G-Secs, for instance. Under normal conditions, the curve slopes upward: longer maturities yield more than shorter ones, reflecting both the

investors demand for tying up money longer, and the market's baseline expectation that growth and inflation will continue, keeping future short-term rates at or above today's level. A flat curve means that premium and those expectations have compressed. An inverted curve, where short-term yields exceed long-term ones, means the market is pricing something more specific: that short-term rates are set to fall in the future.

body.title: Illustrative Shapes: Normal vs Inverted Yield Curve

children.text: Why Inversion Signals Recession Risk, in Theory

Under the expectations hypothesis, a long-term yield is roughly the average of expected future short-term rates over that horizon, plus the term premium. If the market expects the central bank to cut rates meaningfully in the future, because it expects growth or inflation to weaken, that expectation pulls the long end down relative to today's short end. Push that far enough and the curve inverts. The logic is not that the inversion itself causes a recession. It is that professional bond investors, collectively, are pricing in a future rate-cutting cycle, and rate cuts are usually a response to expected economic weakness, not a cause investors would demand ahead of a strong economy.

body.label: US 10Y-2Y Inversion Track Record
body.value: Preceded every US recession since the 1950s
body.context: Widely cited stylised fact, with lead times that have varied considerably, from roughly 6 to over 20 months, and at least one well-known false positive (1966), where inversion was not followed by a recession

body.text: Even in the US, where this signal has the longest and best-documented track record, it comes with real caveats: variable lead times that make it hard to time a portfolio response, and at least one clear false positive. Treat it as a genuine risk signal, not a precise calendar.

children.text: Why India's Yield Curve Doesn't Behave the Same Way

markDefs.definition: A regulatory requirement, set by the RBI, that Indian banks hold a minimum proportion of their net demand and time liabilities in specified liquid assets, overwhelmingly government securities. It creates structural, regulation-driven demand for G-Secs independent of any market view on growth or rates.

children.text: The mechanism above assumes a bond market where prices are set mainly by investors freely expressing a view on future growth and rates. India's G-Sec market has that feature only partially. Banks and insurers are required to hold large quantities of G-Secs through the

and, for insurers, similar regulatory mandates, creating demand that exists regardless of the economic outlook. The government's own borrowing programme, one of the largest in the world relative to GDP, is a major independent driver of long-end supply: a heavier borrowing calendar can push long yields up for fiscal reasons that have nothing to do with growth expectations. Foreign participation in G-Secs has historically been capped and only partially liberalised through routes like the Fully Accessible Route (FAR), limiting how much global rate-view capital can flow in and out to sharpen the curve's signal. And India's corporate bond market remains comparatively shallow, so credit-market information that would otherwise show up as a cleaner corporate curve gets muddled into the sovereign curve instead. Put together, India's long-end yields carry a heavier supply and regulatory imprint than the US curve does, and a lighter pure-expectations imprint.

children.text: The Version of the Spread Actually Used in India

Because outright inversion is rare and India's short-end T-bill market is less continuously liquid than the US 3-month bill market, analysts here watch flattening and compression, not inversion, as the signal. The two spreads used most in practice are the 10-year G-Sec yield against the repo rate, and the 10-year minus 1-year G-Sec spread, both of which are freely available from the RBI's own market data and widely tracked by primary dealers. A sharply compressing 10Y-1Y spread, even without going negative, has historically coincided with periods of policy tightening late in the cycle, consistent with the Peak-phase signature from Lesson 1.4. This course will use this compression-based read throughout, rather than waiting for an outright inversion that may simply not occur even in a genuine slowdown.

body.text: In India, the absence of inversion is not the absence of a signal. A 10Y-1Y spread that has compressed from, say, 150 basis points to near 20 basis points is telling you nearly the same thing a US inversion tells a US analyst, even though it never actually crossed zero. Calibrate your threshold to India's structural reality, not to the US textbook number.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why is outright yield curve inversion a less reliable signal in India than in the United States?
options: Because India's RBI does not set a policy rate the way the US Federal Reserve does

Because regulatory captive demand (SLR), capped foreign participation, and a very large government borrowing programme give India's long-end yields a heavier supply and regulation-driven component, diluting the pure expectations signal
Because India does not publish G-Sec yield data across different maturities
Because Indian investors do not care about future interest rate expectations
body.explanation: The expectations-hypothesis logic behind US curve inversion assumes yields are set mainly by investors pricing future rate expectations. India's SLR-driven captive demand, historically capped foreign access, and a very large borrowing programme all push long-end yields around for reasons unrelated to the growth outlook, which is why flattening, rather than a strict zero-crossing inversion, is the more useful signal here.

body.title: Diagnose the Compression
body.scenario: You notice India's 10Y-1Y G-Sec spread has compressed from 140 basis points to 35 basis points over the past nine months. At the same time, the government has just announced a larger-than-expected borrowing programme for the second half of the fiscal year, and the RBI has raised the repo rate twice in the same period.
body.prompt: Is this compression more likely a genuine growth-expectations signal, a supply-driven distortion, or some combination, and what would you check next to tell the difference?
body.modelAnswer: Most likely some combination, and the RBI's two rate hikes are the part that most supports a genuine growth-expectations read: rising short rates compressing the spread from the short end is consistent with the RBI actively tightening late in the cycle, exactly the Peak-phase pattern from Lesson 1.4. The larger borrowing programme complicates the read, because heavier long-end supply would normally push 10-year yields up, which would widen, not compress, the spread; so if the spread is compressing despite more supply, that is actually a stronger signal that demand-side or growth-expectation forces are dominating. To confirm, check whether the compression is coming mainly from the short end rising (consistent with RBI tightening and a genuine cyclical peak) or from the long end falling despite more supply (which would suggest the market is pricing weaker growth strongly enough to absorb the extra bonds anyway, an even more bearish signal). Either way, cross-check against the other leading indicators from Chapter 1, PMI new orders and credit growth momentum, before acting on the curve signal alone.

body.text: This lesson explains a general analytical framework for reading yield curves, for educational purposes. Yield levels shown in the chart are illustrative, not live market data. This is not investment advice; current G-Sec yields and spreads should always be checked against the RBI's own published data before use.

points: A yield curve inversion reflects the bond market pricing future rate cuts, typically because it expects growth or inflation to weaken, not a direct cause of recession
Even in the US, the signal has variable lead times and at least one notable false positive; it is a risk signal, not a precise calendar

India's G-Sec curve carries a heavier supply and regulatory imprint, via SLR-driven captive demand, capped foreign access, and a very large government borrowing programme, which dilutes the pure expectations signal
Outright inversion is rare in India; flattening and compression in spreads like 10Y-1Y or 10Y-vs-repo are the more useful and more common signal to track
